idiom_name: static fields behind instance methods (JLS class variables)
implementation_notes: Java's translation of the pattern is direct: declare every field private static and keep the accessors non-static, because a class variable is associated with the class rather than with any object and lives in one fixed location in memory, so all instances see the same data while new stays public (Oracle's 'Understanding Class Members'). Nothing replaces the classic structure here - Java has exactly the mechanism the pattern names, which is why the canonical Java write-ups (java-design-patterns.com's LoadBalancer, Martin's Monostate) are literally static fields plus instance methods. Prefer it over Singleton when framework code must instantiate the class itself (JavaBeans, managed containers) or when subclasses should vary behaviour over one shared state; static state cannot be overridden per subclass, and there is no injection seam, so keep it for genuinely application-wide data.
pitfalls: Static fields cannot be overridden: every subclass shares the same variable, so a derivative cannot get its own copy without declaring (and then maintaining) its own storage.

Shared mutable statics are classic test-pollution and thread-bug territory: servers/nextIndex need synchronization (synchronized, AtomicInteger, java.util.concurrent collections) as soon as several threads use different instances.
Static state is per class loader and per JVM: it is not shared across JVMs, and in application servers a redeploy can leave the old and new class loader each holding a copy.
